text:
A: Alright? Can you hear me okay?
B: Yes, fine. Martijn. I'm in Walthamstow.
A: Gareth, Taunton. Nice to meet you. I'll say now, if you hear a beep in the background it's the machine behind me, not my laptop. I'm not on it at the moment, but it likes to remind me it exists.
B: I saw it in the photo. Dialysis?
A: Yeah, home haemodialysis. Five times a week, about four hours a go. I've got the spare room set up as a sort of mini unit. Been on it since my kidneys packed in, so, erm, three years. Sorry, closer to three and a half now.
B: That's a lot of hours.
A: It is. You get used to it. I listen to the cricket mostly. Somerset, if anyone's still asking.
B: I don't follow cricket. I saw the ICE certificate as well. You're a civil engineer?
A: Was. Well, still chartered, I keep the membership going. Drainage and flood defence, mainly, for a consultancy down here. Hydraulic modelling, planning stuff, site meetings in wellies. Had to stop when I went on dialysis. You've got the hard hat, so I'm guessing...?
B: Structural. Associate director at a consultancy in Farringdon. Mostly residential, some mixed-use.
A: Ah, proper buildings. What's on your desk at the moment?
B: A basement extension under a Victorian terrace. The neighbours are difficult and the ground is worse. Groundwater higher than the survey said.
A: Course it is. That's my world, that. Nobody believes the groundwater figures till they've dug the hole. Have you got a decent site investigation, or is it one borehole and a prayer?
B: Two boreholes. Both in the garden, not near the party wall. So, er, sort of a prayer.
A: [laughs] Classic. You'll be designing for the worst case then.
B: I always design for the worst case. The architect thinks I'm being difficult.
A: They always do. I used to have one who'd put a swale through the middle of everything because it looked nice on the render. Then wonder why the levels didn't work.
B: Yes. Pretty drawings.
A: How did you find the puzzle bit at the start?
B: Fine. One of the sequence questions was badly worded. There were two valid answers.
A: The one with the numbers going up by odd steps? I thought that. I put the one I thought they wanted rather than the one I thought was right.
B: I put the right one.
A: [laughs] Fair enough. So, are you from the Netherlands? I'm getting a bit of an accent.
B: Dordrecht. I came for two years. That was twenty-three years ago.
A: Dordrecht. That's all water management, isn't it, round there? Proper envy territory for a flood bloke. I did Amsterdam and Copenhagen before I got ill. Spent most of the time looking at the canals, Hannah'll tell you.
B: Most Dutch people don't think about it. It's just there. My father was a ship's engineer, so I grew up with the river.
A: Do you go back much?
B: A few times a year. Train, I don't fly if I can avoid it. Do you still travel, with the machine?
A: Bits. You have to book holiday dialysis at a unit in advance, so it's Cornwall, the Lakes. If it's not near a unit, we don't go. I'm on the transplant list, two years now, so, you know, fingers crossed. Then I'd like to get back in, maybe freelance, reviewing flood risk assessments.
B: There's demand. Most of the ones I see are poor.
A: That's what I'm counting on.
